title: Fish Whaley, learning to swim, and his father's good earnings
summary: Whaley says he was nicknamed Fish for swimming underwater, and describes his Everett playground, his father's hotel tips and the children's good clothes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And Thomas Whaley, right. Tom Whaley. They used to call me Fish Whaley, because they said I could swim underwater longer than anybody else.
Did you like to swim, Tom?

Oh, yeah. They threw me off -- I used to go down to the bridge where they would swim and see, my mother, she didn't want me to go in the water. One day they threw me in. I stayed away as long as I could so my clothes could dry. And I come home, mama says -- I say, they threw me in the water. Well, then I learned to swim.
What was your mother's name, Tom, again?
Emma.
Emma, that's right.
Yeah, she was --
So then you learned to swim.
Yeah.
You really did swim under water pretty good, huh?
Oh, yeah. We used to just put our faces down and go on through. But we had a great big playground there where we lived.
Where was that?
In Everett.
In Everett, Massachusetts?
Yeah. It's about six or seven miles from Boston. And my father bought a house there, and --
What did your father do, now?
Huh?
What was your father's business? What did you say?

He was in the hotel business, a waiter. He was head waiter of the Bellevue Hotel in Boston. Then he was captain in Young's Hotel, see, and then he became a waiter or a second waiter in -- oh, gee, in a cabaret place where they just serve drinks, see.
But my father used to make a lot of money. In the Bellevue Hotel, he was head water and they would give him money.
That's good.
Every -- when spring come along we'd have a new suit. And in the fall we'd have another suit. See, we were the best-dressed kids in the neighborhood.
How many of you were there?
My --
I'm just rehashing this now.
My -- I had a brother, I had two brothers, one died. And I had two sisters. So there was four of us, and -
That was a nice life as a child.

Oh, yeah. We used to go to school, went to school and I rehashed that, didn't I? Talked about my school days. Yeah. We used to -- when I went to high school I walked two miles. Did I tell you about -- in the choir the man gave me music lessons, and I sang -- used to go to the choir. I'd walk a couple of miles to the choir. And I got my feet wet one winter and I couldn't sing anymore.

I was a kid, about 12, 13 years old. And I could hit E above the staff. I was one of the kids -- the only other kid, he could sing as high as I could, but -- and then one summer we sang over in Trinity Church there in Boston.
That's beautiful.
But in -- I told you about Marva Lewis, I played for her.
